outcome.reply: If a health check fails on a node, it retries once. If that retry also fails, the deploy halts immediately — no more nodes get the new image. The failed node stays on the previous version until someone investigates and either fixes the issue or rolls back.

scenarios.intent:
A room session is history too. The agent said "node-3, moved off node-1" last wake; "it" in the new message refers to the queue worker, and answering at all needs both the pronoun and the session.
Asserted positively on purpose. The first version used a blacklist of ways the agent might ask which machine — and reported 2/3 when all three runs had in fact failed, because two phrased the question in words the blacklist did not contain. A negative assertion only catches the failures you thought of.
The positive version then overshot in the other direction. It asked "can you ssh into it?" and required the reply to contain "node-3" — but a correct answer to that question does not need to name the host. Two runs resolved the pronoun perfectly ("I can run commands on it") and scored as failures, which read as a continuity defect for two cohorts running. The question now asks for the earlier fact directly, so naming it is the answer rather than an optional flourish.

What `summarizeOnTrim` actually buys, measured rather than assumed.
The scenario above is the default path: the trim leaves a marker saying N messages are gone, and the model confabulates a row count anyway in roughly four runs in ten. `summarizeOnTrim` replaces the marker with a summary of what was dropped, at the cost of one extra provider call per trim. This pair is what argued it from off to on by default (#498, measured at 6/12 against 12/12), and it stays here to re-answer the question for every future model rather than settling it once — the flag is pinned on both sides so the row keeps measuring the mechanism rather than whatever the default currently is.
Same history, same budget, same question. The only difference is the flag — which is why the pair can be read as a difference at all.
The assertion is deliberately weaker than its sibling's: a summary may carry the figure across, in which case answering it is correct rather than confabulated. What is still forbidden is the failure both rows share — saying nothing, or saying it through a stall marker.

The control for the summarisation pair, and the reason that pair can argue for a default at all.

scenarios.intent:
Every other row in this file asks the agent to *recall* something from before the trim. This one asks it to act on something: an instruction given at the top of the conversation, whose trigger arrives at the bottom, after the instruction itself has been dropped from the window.
That is the shape of most real standing instructions — "when X happens, do Y" is said once and fires much later — and it is strictly harder than recall. Recall only needs the fact to survive; this needs the fact to survive *and* to be recognised as still binding *and* to be converted into a tool call, with nothing in the final message naming the tool.
It is also the row that says what `summarizeOnTrim` is worth beyond question-answering. A summary that keeps the topic and drops the obligation is useless here and indistinguishable from a good one everywhere else in this file.

Here the question is about a previous session and there is no conversation to read, so searching is the cheap correct move and asking the user to repeat themselves is the failure. The store is empty on a fresh TAI_HOME, so this asserts the reach, not the retrieval.

scenarios.intent:
One message asking two things, each squarely in a different agent's area. Both should answer.
This is the control the rest of this file needs. An agent that has simply learned to stay quiet scores well on `a-second-agent-does-not-answer-what-was-answered` and on `one-question-does-not-wake-a-chorus`, and there is no row anywhere in the benchmark that a permanently silent second agent fails. Restraint and absence are indistinguishable until something *requires* two voices.
